To use per quanto + congiuntivo: per quanto sia difficile.
To use indefinite pronouns and adverbs with the congiuntivo: qualunque cosa succeda, chiunque venga, dovunque tu vada, comunque vada.
To use per + adjective + che + congiuntivo: per lontano che sia.

To use a costo di + infinitive: a costo di venire a nuoto.
To distinguish qualunque (adjective) from qualunque cosa / chiunque (pronoun).
Florence, early March. Three days left before leaving for Malta. Pietro is sitting on the courtyard steps with Lupino. Matei comes and sits next to him.
You've been here for an hour. What's up?
Nothing. I mean… however happy I am for you, I'm sorry you're leaving.
I know. I'm sorry to leave you too. But it's only six months.
Six months without Viola. Whoever wakes her up in the morning, it won't be me.
Let's make a pact. Whatever happens, every Sunday we do a video call.
Even if you were tired? Even if Fiorentina were playing?
Even if Fiorentina were playing Real Madrid. Whatever happens, Sundays are yours.
And in June I'm coming. The professor said that, however expensive the ticket is, he'll pay for it.
Then I'll take you to see the painting. Wherever you want to go, I'll take you.
Even by boat? Grandma says she'll get to Malta even if she has to swim.
Knowing her, she really would. Come on, come inside. It's cold, and Lupino's hungry.
Lupino's always hungry. However much he eats, it's never enough.
"per quanto sia" = however much it is

The last three weeks before the departure flew by, as always happens when you'd like them to last longer. Giulia spent her days in the workshop preparing Chiara: the files on current restorations, the suppliers' numbers, the names of difficult clients, the right way to turn Ernesto's key. Matei packed the suitcases, unpacked them and repacked them, because however hard he tried, he couldn't fit six months of life into three suitcases and a piece of hand luggage. Viola, unaware of everything, kept saying "casa" and pointing at anything, from the fridge to Lupino.

Graziella, on the other hand, had decided to face the departure the way she knew best: by cooking. Every evening she made a different dish, "because in Malta, however well they eat, they don't know how to make pappa al pomodoro". Monday ribollita, Tuesday pappa, Wednesday tripe, Thursday schiacciata with grapes, even though there were no grapes in March and she had bought frozen ones from the baker with some embarrassment. After a week Matei said he would leave five kilos heavier. Graziella replied that this was exactly the point.

On the first weekend of March Ion and Doina arrived too, by train from Sibiu, twenty-six hours of travel to say goodbye to their granddaughter. Doina had been knitting for a whole month, and she pulled six jumpers for Viola out of her suitcase, one for each month away, each a different colour. "I know it's warm in Malta," she said, before anyone could point it out. "But whatever the weather forecasters say, in the evening the wind off the sea is cold. A lady who was there in 1985 told me." Nobody had the courage to contradict her.

Ion, as usual, said little. But on the evening before leaving for Sibiu he sat next to Matei in the courtyard, with his silver railway pocket watch in his hand, and gave it to him. "Take it to Malta," he said in Romanian. "However far you go, it will always show the right time. I've checked it every morning for forty years." Matei tried to refuse: it was his father's most precious possession. Ion shook his head. "Bring it back to me in September," he said. "That way I'm sure you'll come back."

Bellini had a present too. He brought it to the workshop on the second-to-last day, wrapped in a cloth handkerchief, and put it on the table in front of Giulia without a word. It was Ernesto's small brush, the one with the worn handle, which Matei had used for the first brushstroke on the Syracuse Caravaggio. "I can't accept it," said Giulia. "It's the most precious thing in the workshop." "Exactly," replied Bellini. "However small it is, this brush has restored half the Oltrarno. In 1966 it touched the San Frediano Madonna. Two years ago it touched Saint Lucy. Now it must touch Saint John. Whatever you decide to do with it, bring it back to me in September. Clean." Giulia wrapped it in the handkerchief again and put it in her bag, in the safest place, next to the passports.

The two grandmothers, meanwhile, had found a way to spend the last days together. Doina spoke hardly any Italian and Graziella didn't know a word of Romanian, but however much of an obstacle the language was, the kitchen was not. They spent a whole afternoon at the stove: Doina taught Graziella to make sarmale, the cabbage rolls Matei ate as a child, and Graziella taught her the secret of ribollita, which nobody knew except her and, since August, Assunta. Then, in the evening, Doina sang Graziella Viorica's lullaby, slowly, word by word, until Graziella knew it by heart. "So," said Doina with her hands, "when the little one calls, you sing."

Pietro was the one who suffered most, although he didn't say so. In three years he had got used to having Viola upstairs: hearing her run across the floor in the morning, taking her to the market with Grandma, teaching her new words. Now, whatever he did, it seemed to him he was doing it for the last time. The last breakfast together. The last Saturday at the open workshop with Matei. The last walk with Lupino along the Arno. In the evenings he sat on the courtyard steps, with the dog beside him, looking at the window of Viola's little room.

That's where Matei found him, three days before the departure, and that's where they made the pact. A video call every Sunday at seven in the evening, whatever happened, even if Fiorentina were playing. In June, once school was over, Pietro would go to Malta for two weeks, with the ticket given by Bellini. And until then Pietro would have an important task: keeping Viola's little room in order, "so that when she comes back, she finds everything as it was". Pietro accepted with the seriousness of a minister.

The last evening there was a farewell dinner, at the trattoria, of course. Everyone came, even people nobody had invited: Lorenzo with a cake in the shape of Malta, rather imprecise, Rita and Davide, Signor Franco with his paddle, Valeria, Mancini with his recorder "for the archive", the prior with cantucci, and even Rocco, the Calabrian foreman, who was passing by chance and stayed until midnight. Bellini made a short speech, for once. "However sorry I am to see you go," he said, "I'm happy. Whoever leaves this workshop for Malta leaves a little for me too."

Chiara, who from the next day would be director of the workshop, couldn't say anything. She hugged Giulia so hard that her glasses fell off. Davide, on the other hand, had prepared a present: a framed drawing of the workshop, with everyone in it, Bellini in his corner, Chiara at the big table, himself with the lamp, Pietro in the doorway, Lupino under a table. And in the background, small, hanging on the wall like two paintings, Giulia and Matei with Viola in their arms. "That way, wherever you are," he said, blushing, "you're always here too."

Later, when the guests began to leave, Chiara took Giulia aside in the kitchen, among the pots. "I'm scared," she confessed quietly. "However much you've prepared me, tomorrow morning I open the workshop alone. What if I get something wrong? What if a difficult client turns up? What if the professor is taken ill again?" Giulia took her hands. "Chiara, listen to me. Whatever happens, call me. At any hour. But you won't, because wherever you're put, you cope. You proved it with the angel and with the banner. And however it goes, the workshop won't collapse in six months. It's been standing since 1952." Chiara laughed through her tears. "The trattoria's been there since 1952," she said. "The workshop is older." "Exactly," replied Giulia. "It's survived worse than you."

On the morning of the departure, at six, Via Maggio was still dark. Marco loaded the suitcases into the car, helped by Pietro, who hadn't slept. Graziella came down with an enormous flask on which she had stuck a handwritten label: "Herbal tea". Matei looked at it suspiciously. "Grandma, what's inside?" Graziella put on the most innocent face in the world. "Herbal tea," she repeated. "For the journey. Whatever happens at security, say it's herbal tea." Giulia laughed for the first time in days. It was the same strategy she had used with Bellini's broth in hospital.

Saying goodbye on the pavement was harder than expected, although everyone had promised not to cry. Graziella took Viola in her arms and held her tight for a long moment, smelling her hair the way you smell freshly baked bread. Viola, who didn't understand why everyone's eyes were red, kissed her on the nose and said, in her most serious voice: "Grandma. Herbal tea." Graziella burst out laughing and crying at the same time. "Good girl," she said. "Herbal tea. Mind you don't tell anyone what's inside."

Pietro had prepared a speech, but when his turn came not a word came out. So he did something different. He took from his pocket his school exercise book, the one with Grandpa Aldo's sentences copied out in July, and gave it to Giulia. "For the restoration diary," he said. "All the subjunctives are right. In case in Malta you forget how to write in Italian." Giulia hugged him tight, without a word. Matei ruffled his hair. "Sunday at seven," he said. "Even if Real Madrid are playing." "Even if Real Madrid are playing," repeated Pietro.

At Pisa airport the flask got through security without any trouble. The officer opened it, sniffed, and screwed the lid back on with a strange expression, somewhere between surprise and nostalgia. "Herbal tea?" he asked. "Herbal tea," confirmed Matei, poker-faced. The officer looked at him for a long second, then smiled. "My grandmother used to make herbal tea like this too," he said. "With cavolo nero." And he let them through. Giulia described the scene to Graziella on the phone from the departure lounge. Graziella said it was the final proof: however much the world changes, ribollita opens every door.

They landed in Malta at noon, under a sky so blue it looked painted. Camilleri was waiting for them at the airport again, this time with Marija and a bunch of flowers for Viola. The apartment with the green gallarija was ready: Marija had filled the fridge, put flowers on the table and left on Viola's bed a hand-made woollen blanket, "because in the evening, whatever they say, the wind off the sea is cold". Giulia and Matei looked at each other and burst out laughing. Doina and Marija, without ever having met, had said exactly the same thing.

That evening, on the terrace, they opened the "herbal tea" flask and ate Graziella's ribollita looking at the harbour, still lukewarm after ten hours of travel. Viola fell asleep with her bunny and Doina's blue jumper, the first of the six. Matei took out Ion's watch and put it on the table: it showed a quarter past nine, exactly, like the clock on the bell tower opposite. "See?" he said to Giulia. "However far away we are, the time is the same." Giulia took his hand. "The time, yes," she replied. "The rest we'll find out tomorrow."

The next day, at eight in the morning, Giulia walked into the oratory of the Co-Cathedral for her first day of work. The technicians had already put up scaffolding in front of the painting, as high as a three-storey house, with lamps and microscopes. Camilleri introduced her to the team: two Maltese restorers, a chemist from Palermo, a Japanese photographer who spoke only English and a young apprentice called Karl, who immediately reminded Giulia of Davide. Then he gave her the keys. Giulia climbed the scaffolding, went up to the signature, opened her bag and took out the handkerchief with Ernesto's brush. However hard she tried, she couldn't stop smiling. "Right," she said aloud, in Italian, to the saint. "Let's begin. One millimetre at a time."

The following Sunday, at seven on the dot, Matei's phone rang. On the screen appeared Pietro's face, too close to the camera, and behind him, one after another, everyone else's: Graziella, Marco, Bellini, Chiara, Davide, Lupino licking the screen. In the trattoria they had propped the phone on a pile of plates, and everyone was pushing to get into the frame. "You said even if Real Madrid were playing," said Pietro, very seriously. "Tonight Fiorentina are playing. And I'm here." Matei laughed. "So am I," he replied. "However the match goes, we've already won." Pietro, on the other side of the screen, gave a thumbs up, and for a moment Florence and Valletta seemed like the same city.
